query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Nb (~2 wt%) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy to form finely dispersed, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates at the grain boundaries will reinforce the load‐bearing integrity, limiting crack initiation and propagation, while leaving the caloric response largely intact under magnetic and pressure field operation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric effect but poor load-bearing integrity with a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~2 wt% Nb during the melting process followed by a homogenization and aging heat treatment designed to precipitate fine, coherent Nb-rich nanoparticles at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under operating regimes relevant to solid refrigeration: magnetic fields up to the device-applied field strength, pressure fields typical of the refrigeration cycle, temperatures near the caloric transition point (typically ambient or slightly below), and standard mechanical loading (tensile/fracture toughness tests) at ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a network of nanoprecipitates at the grain boundaries that act as barriers to crack propagation and improve fracture toughness.
generation.mechanism: Nb microalloying promotes a precipitation strengthening mechanism by nucleating Nb-rich particles at the grain boundaries. These particles arrest crack growth and improve ductility and toughness. This intervention is anticipated to have minimal influence on the phase transitions that drive the caloric response, thereby preserving the magneto- and barocaloric effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the fracture toughness and overall load-bearing integrity (e.g., a target improvement of >10%) while retaining the magnitude of the caloric response (within approximately 5–10% of the baseline performance).
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, known for its large caloric response but poor mechanical integrity and tendency to crack.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold under the same magnetic and pressure fields as used in refrigeration cycles, within the temperature window of the caloric phase transformation, and under ambient loading conditions during mechanical testing.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the precise quantitative impact of Nb addition on the caloric transition temperature and the magnitude of the caloric effect. The microalloying may also slightly alter the transformation kinetics, so detailed characterization is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of materials: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with a 2 wt% Nb addition processed through identical melting, homogenization, and aging steps, and a control set without Nb. Evaluate both sets under identical operating conditions.
measurements: Fracture toughness (KIC) and mechanical load-bearing tests (tensile strength, crack propagation analysis)
Caloric performance tests including magnetically induced entropy change and adiabatic temperature change under specified magnetic and pressure fields
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess any shifts in transformation temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the Nb-modified alloy fails to exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., an increase of less than 10% in fracture toughness) or if the caloric performance is degraded by more than approximately 10% compared to the control alloy under the defined field, pressure, and temperature conditions.
